slides.title: Wind can release flight without initiating every take-off
body: A locust can begin wing beating when airflow reaches the wind-sensitive hairs on its head. In **tethered flight**, the animal is held in place, so an experimenter controls airflow independently of the animal’s forward movement. This preparation isolates sensory conditions that can release flight.

Camhi filmed freely jumping _Schistocerca gregaria_ at 64 frames per second and compared wing opening with wind-triggered responses in tethered animals. Wings began opening within approximately 15 ms of jump onset, whereas the fastest measured response to wind took 35 ms.

Wind stimulation is therefore sufficient for flight initiation under tethered conditions but is too slow to explain the initial wing opening in these jumps. A sensory stimulus that can release a behavior need not be the natural trigger on every occasion.

slides.title: Elevators and depressors alternate with a hindwing lead
body: **Elevator muscles** raise the wings; **depressor muscles** lower them. Forewings attach to the mesothorax and hindwings to the metathorax, the second and third thoracic segments. A motor neuron is a nerve cell whose axon activates a muscle.

Wilson described flight near 17 wingbeats per second, with hindwing activation leading corresponding forewing activation by approximately 6–8 ms. The flight motor score alternated elevators and depressors while coordinating both body sides. The upstroke occupied about 41% of a normal cycle.

These relationships define an organized motor pattern rather than undifferentiated muscle excitation. Later deafferented preparations retained alternation and a hindwing lead, but their measured delays depended on the experimental treatment. Intact movement timing and reduced-preparation muscle timing are related measurements with different mechanical conditions.

slides.title: Head airflow changes downstroke wing twist
body: **Pronation** is wing rotation toward the orientation used during the downstroke; **supination** is the reverse rotation associated with the upstroke. Wing twist changes the wing’s interaction with air and therefore contributes to lift control.

Camhi delivered 0–4 m/s airflow to the head of tethered locusts while shielding the body and wings. Stroboscopic photographs measured a paper marker across the forewing chord. Faster head airflow reduced downstroke pronation, whereas upstroke twist changed little.

Directing wind at the wing instead of the head did not reproduce the response. This control supports a sensory-mediated adjustment rather than a direct aerodynamic twisting effect. The head-wind experiment measured wing angle, so the corresponding change in lift remained a functional interpretation rather than a simultaneous force measurement.

slides.title: Jump-associated wing opening outruns the wind reflex
body: Camhi monitored airflow with a hot-wire anemometer and detected wing opening when the forewing stopped interrupting a narrow light beam. Both signals were photographed on the same moving film. This method placed stimulus onset and movement onset on a common time base.

Wind accelerations of 100–600 m/s² ended at speeds of 2.5–4.5 m/s. Typical wing-opening latency was approximately 45 ms, and the shortest measured latency was 35 ms. Freely jumping animals had begun opening their wings within approximately 15 ms.

Covering the head hairs prevented wind-triggered opening; removing the covering restored it. The hairs therefore supplied the tested reflex pathway. The latency difference supports an additional jump-associated initiating pathway, while the behavioral experiment alone does not identify its neurons.

slides.title: Removing foot contact releases a slower initiation route
body: The **tarsi** are the distal portions of the legs that contact a surface. Contact can inhibit flight in a tethered locust. Camhi placed the animal on a hinged roughened rod and lowered the rod to remove support while recording the first wing-opening movement.

Wing opening followed the last possible instant of contact by at least 30 ms. The latency remained similar after successive leg amputations, including trials with only one leg contacting the rod. The support was mechanically independent of the tether, and comparable hand movements did not release flight.

Loss of contact can therefore release flight under these conditions, but its latency is longer than jump-associated wing opening. The controls reduce explanations based on shock to the tether or insufficient initial contact. They do not identify the central pathway that couples jumping to flying.

slides.title: Head hairs form a directional mechanosensory array
body: A **mechanoreceptor** converts mechanical displacement into neural activity. The locust’s aerodynamic head hairs are **setae**, cuticular shafts coupled to sensory cells. Their shafts are approximately 70–250 μm long and curve forward in different directions.

Camhi mapped the curvature of the larger hairs and compared individual hair orientation with sensory responses. A receptor responded most strongly when wind arrived in the plane of its shaft curvature. The array was approximately bilaterally symmetrical and similar across animals.

Different preferred directions allow the head to distribute airflow information across receptors. A single receptor’s firing rate still depends on both wind direction and speed, so it is not an unambiguous speed meter. The anatomical map predicts preferred direction but does not measure the full response of every smaller hair.

slides.title: Sustained wind produces adapting sensory discharge
body: **Adaptation** is a decline in a receptor’s response during a maintained stimulus. Camhi teased small axon bundles from the circumoesophageal connective and recorded a sensory unit during controlled airflow. These connectives run beside the oesophagus between head ganglia.

A 4.5 m/s wind directed approximately 10° left of center produced an initial discharge near 200 spikes/s. Within about half a second, the rate declined to a maintained level near 125 spikes/s. Continued airflow produced a further modest decline over minutes.

The sensory discharge contains both an onset response and information about continuing airflow. Adaptation does not imply complete loss of sensitivity. Because these recordings were extracellular, they establish action-potential timing but do not directly measure the receptor current or identify its mechanically gated ion channel.

slides.title: One hair encodes direction and speed together
body: Camhi rotated a calibrated wind jet around the head and recorded the maintained firing of a single sensory axon. A **directional tuning curve** relates neural response to stimulus direction. Different wind speeds were tested with the same receptor.

The published curves used 1.5, 3.0 and 4.5 m/s wind. Maximum firing occurred near 15° left of center, close to the hair’s measured curvature plane. The angular separation between the half-maximum responses was approximately 54°, and higher speeds produced higher firing rates.

The rate therefore combines direction and speed rather than representing either variable alone. The alignment of response and shaft curvature links anatomy to sensory tuning. These measurements do not establish the decoding operation performed by downstream interneurons or behaviorally achievable angular precision.

slides.title: Several mechanical asymmetries sharpen hair tuning
body: Camhi separated three potential sources of directional tuning: shaft curvature, socket elasticity, and the off-center attachment of the receptor dendrite. Mechanical displacement with a pipette controlled the shaft movement directly, reducing the contribution of aerodynamic drag.

A 50 μm shaft deflection produced a broader directional response than wind stimulation. Its typical half-maximum width was approximately 85°, compared with approximately 54° for the wind response. Measurements of socket resistance and drag on remounted shafts were broader still.

No tested component alone accounted for the narrow wind-tuning curve. The results support combined contributions from mechanical structure and sensory coupling. They do not identify the molecular transduction channel, and the remounted-shaft experiment depended on the mechanical properties of the replacement socket.

slides.title: Head-hair axons reach the suboesophageal ganglion
body: Camhi recorded simultaneously from a cut hair tip and an axon in the ipsilateral circumoesophageal connective. **Ipsilateral** means on the same side; **contralateral** means on the opposite side. Every recorded sensory impulse appeared at both sites.

The two recordings were separated by approximately 10 ms. Electrical stimulation of the connective evoked impulses that traveled back toward the hair, with latencies of 7–14 ms and an estimated conduction speed near 0.5 m/s. Stimulation farther back in the cervical connective did not evoke the same sensory response.

These tests support axons passing through the brain and terminating before the thoracic pathway, probably in the suboesophageal ganglion. The physiological inference is stronger than visual proximity alone. It does not reconstruct every terminal branch or directly identify each sensory-to-interneuron synapse.

slides.title: Wind-indicator interneurons pool broad directional input
body: An **interneuron** connects other neurons rather than directly serving as the primary receptor or muscle output. Camhi recorded individual wind-responsive units in the cervical connective, downstream of the head sensory pathways. Wind-indicator cells sustained discharge during maintained airflow.

Their directional half-maximum width was approximately 140°, substantially broader than individual sensory receptors. At favorable direction, a 4.5 m/s wind produced a maintained rate near 85 spikes/s. Small air jets mapped inputs from head hairs on both sides with varied preferred directions.

Pooling differently tuned receptors is consistent with a broad signal for the presence and intensity of airflow. The recordings and receptive-field tests do not directly establish the exact synaptic weights. Camhi’s classification described response properties rather than assigning each unit a modern identified-cell label.

slides.title: Wind-direction cells retain sharper angular preferences
body: Camhi distinguished wind-direction cells from broadly tuned wind-indicator cells by varying wind angle, speed and angular motion. The recorded units maintained firing in wind but had sharper angular selectivity. Their mapped sensory inputs had more similar preferred directions.

Directional half-maximum widths were approximately 60°. Rotating an already flowing jet toward a cell’s favorable direction could add a transient burst, whereas moving away could briefly reduce discharge. The rate-speed relationship was not simply linear across the tested range.

A downstream cell can therefore emphasize directional information while remaining sensitive to stimulus strength and change. These findings support a possible role in directional stabilization, but Camhi did not prove that a particular recorded unit was necessary for a specific yaw-correction movement.

slides.title: Recentre cells emphasize motion toward head-on airflow
body: **Recentre cells** are Camhi’s rapidly adapting interneurons that respond especially to airflow shifting toward the head-on direction from one preferred side. He pivoted a maintained wind jet around the head rather than repeatedly turning airflow on and off.

At 3 m/s, a shift toward center from the preferred side evoked a burst, while the reverse shift or recentring from the other side could evoke little activity. Rapid shifts were more effective than slow shifts; strong responses occurred for pivots lasting less than about 100–150 ms.

The response distinguishes the direction of a change, beyond the starting and ending wind angles alone. The preparation establishes temporal and directional selectivity. A role in terminating corrective turns was proposed from these properties, but not verified by selective cell manipulation.

slides.title: Acceleration cells emphasize rapid airflow onset
body: Camhi tested acceleration-sensitive interneurons by increasing wind from rest to the same final speed over different time intervals. **Acceleration** is the rate of change of velocity. Fixing the final speed distinguished sensitivity to onset dynamics from sensitivity to maintained speed.

These cells responded only when wind reached approximately 1–1.5 m/s or more. Faster acceleration toward 4.5 m/s produced shorter initial interspike intervals and a more vigorous burst. Directional tuning was broad, and even sizable angular pivots of an existing wind jet could fail to evoke activity.

Their response therefore differs from both sustained wind-indication and directional recentring. It is consistent with a transient signal about airflow onset. The recordings do not establish that acceleration cells alone initiate flight, especially because free-jump wing opening occurs faster than the tested wind reflex.

slides.title: Flight-like alternation survives loss of wing feedback
body: A **central pattern generator**, or CPG, can generate rhythmic patterned output without requiring rhythmic sensory input. Wilson progressively removed wings, cut wing sensory nerves, and reduced the preparation to the head and thoracic nervous system, with limited remaining body structures.

Continuous wind at the head still elicited alternating elevator and depressor activity. Reduced preparations produced approximately 4–12 cycles/s, often near 7 cycles/s. Elevator-to-depressor delays remained around 30–40 ms in well-preserved preparations, despite the slower overall rhythm.

Wing movement and its feedback were therefore unnecessary for the basic alternation. This does not mean that feedback is unnecessary for normal frequency, aerodynamic control or stable free flight. Continuous sensory excitation from the head supplied activation without specifying every phase of the rhythm.

slides.title: Thoracic motor axons burst without flight muscles
body: Wilson recorded from motor nerves in preparations lacking thoracic muscles and the abdomen. A **motor axon** carries the neural output toward muscle; recording its central stump tests whether rhythmic drive is produced before muscle contraction occurs.

Small bursts of spikes repeated at approximately 4–10 cycles/s. Activity in the two wing-related segments was often nearly synchronous or separated by a few milliseconds, though timing could drift over long periods. Some preparations had an irregular mesothoracic rhythm while metathoracic discharge remained orderly.

Rhythm without attached flight muscles excludes a muscle-driven reflex chain as the sole origin of the recorded bursts. The reduced output still differed from intact flight. Preparation damage and lost feedback limit conclusions about the normal precision and contributions of each segment.

slides.title: Unpatterned excitation can release patterned output
body: Wilson stimulated the anterior thoracic cord electrically while recording flight muscle responses in reduced preparations. A **tonic drive** is sustained excitation that need not repeat at the same rhythm as the motor output. Stimulation frequency and output frequency were varied independently.

Repeated stimulation could recruit alternating groups of motor activity instead of a simple one-for-one muscle response. At slower stimulation rates, some units followed the stimulus directly; at higher rates, the circuit produced a rhythm with its own changing frequency. The response depended on the recruited pathways and preparation state.

Central circuitry can therefore transform continuing excitation into patterned alternation. This experiment does not require a single dedicated pacemaker neuron. Electrical cord stimulation recruits multiple axons, so it cannot identify the natural activating cell or its transmitter.

slides.title: The 404 group links sensory input to flight activation
body: Pearson and colleagues recorded and dye-filled **404 interneurons** in _Locusta migratoria_. These mesothoracic cells have looping main neurites and ascending axons. A neurite is a neuronal process; dye filling linked the physiological recordings to recognizable anatomy.

slides.title: 404 discharge tracks the frequency of fictive flight
body: In Pearson and colleagues’ preparation, the discharge rate of a 404 neuron declined during a sustained wind stimulus as the frequency of flight activity declined. **Fictive flight** is flight-like neural or muscle output in a reduced preparation, rather than aerodynamic flight through space.

Higher 404 firing rates were associated with faster flight rhythms. Turning the lights off increased both 404 activity and rhythm frequency while preserving the relationship between them. Flight commonly ended after the recorded 404 discharge fell below approximately 50 spikes/s.

The association is consistent with an excitatory drive that regulates circuit activation. Correlation alone does not prove that 404 firing causes the frequency change, because both could respond to another input. Current-injection experiments supplied the additional causal test.

slides.title: Depolarizing one 404 neuron can initiate the flight rhythm
body: **Depolarization** makes membrane voltage less negative and can increase neuronal firing. Pearson and colleagues injected depolarizing current into a single 404 neuron while recording dorsal longitudinal muscle activity and, in additional trials, an elevator or depressor motor neuron.

Current-evoked rhythms commonly started near 8 cycles/s, slower than the approximately 12 cycles/s initially recorded during wind-induced episodes. Motor-neuron voltage oscillations resembled those evoked by wind.

slides.title: Hyperpolarizing one 404 neuron can prevent initiation
body: **Hyperpolarization** makes membrane voltage more negative and can suppress firing. Pearson and colleagues compared a brief wind pulse before and during hyperpolarizing current injection into a recorded 404 neuron. The stimulus was otherwise unchanged.

A 0.5 s wind pulse normally evoked a short flight episode. During approximately 6 nA of hyperpolarizing current, the recorded 404 cell produced only one impulse and the same stimulus failed to initiate the flight rhythm. Suppression was most effective with weaker wind or near the end of an episode.

A single member of the activating group can therefore influence whether the circuit reaches its activation threshold. The condition dependence prevents interpreting this as universal necessity of one cell. Other 404 neurons and parallel inputs can contribute enough drive under stronger stimulation.

slides.title: 404 bursts may link jumping to the start of flight
body: Pearson and colleagues recorded a 404 neuron together with hindleg muscle activity during kicks. A kick uses coordinated flexor and extensor activation followed by rapid extension. Its motor organization resembles that used to launch a jump.

The source of the kick-associated excitation was unresolved. These recordings were not direct proof that 404 neurons trigger wing opening during natural jumps.

slides.title: Interneuron 301 can advance or delay the next cycle
body: A neuron’s rhythmic firing does not by itself establish that it helps generate the rhythm. Robertson and Pearson injected brief current pulses into identified interneuron 301 during fictive flight and measured the timing of subsequent dorsal longitudinal motor bursts.

A 30 ms depolarizing pulse could advance or delay the next cycle depending on when it occurred. **Phase** specifies the position within a repeating cycle; a **phase-response curve** relates the timing of a perturbation to its effect on the rhythm. The neuron’s branches span mesothoracic and metathoracic regions.

Phase-dependent resetting supplies causal evidence for participation in rhythm generation. It does not prove that 301 is the sole oscillator or that the tested pulse reproduces its natural synaptic input. The response must be interpreted within the connected flight network.

slides.title: Interneuron 501 supplies phase-dependent delays
body: Robertson and Pearson tested interneuron 501 with the same phase-dependent current-injection approach used for 301. The dye-filled cell was identified within the metathoracic ganglion. Both neurons expressed flight-related activity, but their resetting effects differed.

Brief depolarizing pulses into 501 reliably delayed the following cycle over particular phases. Apparent advances were not clearly separable from ordinary cycle variation. Its inhibitory connections included elevator-related pathways, whereas its own burst was associated with the depressor phase.

The distinction between 301 and 501 argues against treating every rhythmically active interneuron as functionally interchangeable. 501 can alter when the network moves into its next cycle. Current injection establishes a network effect while leaving other neurons and parallel oscillatory mechanisms available.

slides.title: Delayed excitation and fast inhibition couple 301 and 501
body: Robertson and Pearson recorded simultaneously from interneurons 301 and 501. A **postsynaptic potential** is a change in membrane voltage caused by input from another neuron. An excitatory potential tends to favor firing; an inhibitory potential tends to oppose it under the recorded conditions.

A spike in 301 preceded a depolarizing potential in 501 by approximately 6 ms. A spike in 501 preceded an inhibitory potential in 301 by approximately 3 ms. The delayed excitation lasted longer than the feedback inhibition and could support alternating activation and release from inhibition.

These paired recordings establish directional physiological interactions. A longer latency suggests additional processing but does not alone count synapses. The 301-to-501 depolarization required further tests because depolarization can arise from removal of inhibition rather than direct excitatory transmitter action.

slides.title: A depolarizing response can arise from disinhibition
body: **Disinhibition** is excitation caused by reducing an inhibitory influence. Robertson and Pearson hyperpolarized 501 while monitoring its delayed response to 301 spikes. The delayed depolarizing potential decreased and reversed sign near 6 nA of hyperpolarizing current. Spontaneous inhibitory potentials reversed at a similar point. Chloride loading reduced the delayed potential, consistent with an inhibitory conductance contributing to its origin.

An identified pathway through interneuron 511 contained inhibition from 301 to 511 and from 511 to 501. The observations support delayed excitation through disinhibition, but tonic graded transmitter release at the candidate intermediate connection was not directly established.

slides.title: Picrotoxin disrupts inhibition and delayed excitation
body: Robertson and Pearson applied **picrotoxin**, an inhibitor of certain ligand-gated inhibitory channel responses, to test the proposed disinhibitory pathway. The bath concentration was approximately 150 μM. Paired recordings compared the same connections before and after treatment.

Within about 4 min, picrotoxin blocked inhibition from 301 to 511 and also the delayed excitation from 301 to 501. Neuron 501 became strongly depolarized and could fire continuously. Rhythmic activity sometimes persisted at 16–18 Hz instead of the usual 10–12 Hz, with altered bursts and disrupted phase relationships.

Blocking an inhibitory influence can remove a depolarizing response that depends on disinhibition. The result supports that mechanism but does not identify a particular inhibitory transmitter or receptor subunit. Persistent, distorted rhythmicity also argues against assigning all oscillation to this one interaction.

slides.title: Interneuron chains carry CPG timing to depressor output
body: A **premotor interneuron** influences motor neurons, placing it between network timing and muscle activation. Robertson and Pearson found delayed excitation from 301 to interneuron 503, followed by excitation from 503 to 201. The 201 cells provide excitatory input to depressor motor neurons.

Paired intracellular recordings linked 301 spikes to delayed 503 responses and 503 spikes to shorter-latency 201 responses. The two stages preserve a separation between elevator-associated activity in 301 and later depressor-associated drive. Their recordings include millivolt voltage and millisecond time calibrations.

The chain supplies a physiological route by which central activity can establish phase relationships in motor output. It is part of a broader network, with additional excitation and inhibition. The recorded connections do not establish that the chain is the only route to every depressor motor neuron.

slides.title: Muscarinic stimulation recruits a flight-like motor score
body: **Acetylcholine** is a neurotransmitter acting through nicotinic and muscarinic receptors. Muscarinic receptors are G-protein-coupled receptors that alter cellular signaling and excitability. An **agonist** activates a receptor; pilocarpine is a muscarinic agonist used to test flight activation.

Pilocarpine induced alternating activity after several seconds, with pauses interrupting the flight episodes. Wind-induced activity served as the reference pattern.

The agonist establishes that muscarinic stimulation can recruit the flight circuitry without phasic wing feedback. Bath sufficiency does not identify the endogenous releasing neuron, local transmitter concentration, or receptor subtype. The retained muscle arrangement and phase relationships distinguish a flight score from general hyperactivity.

slides.title: Nicotinic excitation alone does not recruit stable flight
body: **Nicotinic receptors** are ligand-gated ion channels activated by acetylcholine and nicotine. Unlike muscarinic receptors, they mediate direct channel responses. Buhl and colleagues compared nicotine with **carbachol**, an acetylcholine analogue that activates both receptor classes.

At 1 mM, nicotine produced a brief burst of uncoordinated motor activity rather than a stable flight pattern. At 5 mM, carbachol produced sustained flight-like alternation near 18 Hz. This was faster than the approximately 11.5 Hz rhythm induced by pilocarpine in the same study.

Direct excitation of motor activity is therefore insufficient evidence for CPG recruitment. Combined muscarinic and nicotinic actions may support faster output, but the experiment did not isolate every cellular contribution. The nicotinic antagonist tests were not selectively reversible at doses that abolished activity.

slides.title: Muscarinic antagonists reversibly block wind initiation
body: An **antagonist** reduces a receptor’s response to its activating ligand. Buhl and colleagues perfused the thoracic nervous system with 10 mM atropine or scopolamine, both muscarinic antagonists. Wind stimulation and pilocarpine were tested during the treatment.

Reversibility reduces an explanation based solely on irreversible tissue damage. Blockade of natural stimulation and an agonist supports a necessary muscarinic step in the tested pathway. High bath doses and the absence of cell-specific receptor manipulation limit assignment of the affected receptor to a particular interneuron.

slides.title: TCG-driven flight also requires muscarinic signaling
body: The **tritocerebral commissure giant interneuron**, or TCG, is a descending wind-responsive neuron with an axon approximately 20 μm in diameter. A commissure connects structures across the nervous system’s midline. Buhl and colleagues stimulated its accessible axon while monitoring flight muscle activity.

body: **Biogenic amines** are signaling molecules that can modulate neural activity; octopamine, dopamine and tyramine are examples. Buhl and colleagues applied them to deafferented preparations and compared their motor patterns with wind- and cholinergic-induced activity.

slides.title: Flight initiation persists after verified amine depletion
body: **Reserpine** reduces stored biogenic amines and provides a test distinct from receptor-antagonist application. Buhl and colleagues injected a total of 500 μg per locust over two treatments. slides.title: Activation chemistry changes frequency and phase together
body: Buhl and colleagues quantified the motor score with simultaneous recordings from a hindwing elevator and several depressor muscles. **Cycle frequency** is the number of complete repetitions per second; **phase** expresses where one event falls within that repetition.

Wind-induced fictive flight averaged approximately 8.6 Hz, pilocarpine-induced activity 11.5 Hz, and carbachol-induced activity 18.1 Hz. The elevator occupied phase approximately 0.58 with wind and 0.52 with pilocarpine, but approximately 0.76 during octopamine-induced activity.

Similar alternating patterns therefore need not have identical temporal structure. The chemistry used to release a motor program can also tune the program. These values describe deafferented preparations and should not be treated as interchangeable with the frequency, forces or wing angles of intact flight.

slides.title: Tegula input resets the transition to wing elevation
body: The **tegula** is a proprioceptive sense organ at the wing base that signals wing downstroke. **Proprioception** supplies information about the animal’s own movement. Ausborn and colleagues electrically stimulated hindwing tegula afferents while monitoring wing position and elevator motor-neuron voltage.

Stimulus trains used 0.1 ms pulses at 220 Hz to approximate natural receptor bursts. Stimulating at different phases synchronized the subsequent elevator response and wing movement. Excitatory postsynaptic potential amplitudes varied within a flight episode even when stimulation occurred at similar phases.

The tegula can therefore reset a centrally generated rhythm instead of merely reporting its movement. The response depends on circuit state and effective sensory input. Electrical activation substitutes for natural hair movement, so it does not reproduce every mechanical detail of the intact wing-base receptor.

slides.title: Recruiting more tegula afferents increases central input
body: Ausborn and colleagues stimulated the cut tegula nerve while recording its **compound action potential**, the summed extracellular response of several axons. The lowest stimulus voltage producing a detectable response defined threshold T. Increasing voltage recruited additional afferents.

A second nerve-response component appeared near 1.3 times threshold in the published example. Higher stimulus intensities also produced larger postsynaptic responses in flight interneurons, including 511. The recordings distinguish increasing peripheral recruitment from an assumed change in one neuron’s spike size.

Stimulus strength is therefore an experimentally controlled way to change the sensory drive reaching the network. It is not a direct measurement of natural synaptic gain at one identified receptor connection. The resulting network response must also be assessed with feedback timing allowed to depend on motor output.

slides.title: Closed-loop feedback strength can slow the flight rhythm
body: In **closed-loop feedback**, motor output affects the next sensory input, which then affects later motor output. Ausborn and colleagues used depressor muscle bursts to calculate the onset and duration of each subsequent tegula stimulus train in real time.

Near threshold, feedback sped the rhythm from approximately 10.3 to 13.1 Hz in the published example. Raising stimulation from 0.75 V to 1.5 V, twice threshold, greatly reduced that acceleration. In some preparations strong feedback slowed the rhythm below its unstimulated frequency.

Stronger sensory excitation does not therefore guarantee a faster closed-loop rhythm. Timing, stimulus duration and network inhibition interact across cycles. The experimental recordings confirm a feedback-dependent relationship predicted by a model, but they do not establish every ionic current assumed by that model.

slides.title: Walking and flight circuits can operate simultaneously
body: Rillich and colleagues recorded leg motor nerves and wing muscle activity from the same deafferented locust. **Co-activation** means that two motor programs are expressed together. The preparation retained motor output but removed sensory and descending inputs that ordinarily help select locomotion.

At 1 mM pilocarpine, slow walking-like bursts in leg pathways could occur at the same time as rapid flight-like wing alternation. Walking activity often began within approximately 1 min of drug application and flight activity followed after approximately 1–3 min. Individual leg spikes could become coupled to wingbeats within the slow step rhythm.

The two CPGs can therefore remain active concurrently in a reduced nervous system. This does not mean that intact locusts normally walk and fly simultaneously. Behavioral exclusivity can depend on additional selection mechanisms rather than obligatory inhibition between the core rhythm generators.

slides.title: Octopamine and tyramine recruit different motor states
body: Rillich and colleagues compared **octopamine** with **tyramine**, its biosynthetic precursor and an independent signaling molecule. Both could activate flight-related output, but their effects on leg motor patterns differed. The same preparation and recorded pathways were used for the comparison.

Octopamine at 100 mM strongly recruited flight-like wing activity and usually coupled leg motor units to the flight rhythm. Tyramine at 10 mM could recruit walking-like activity; a higher 100 mM concentration could recruit flight as well. Leg-wing coupling was weaker during tyramine-induced activity.

The effect of an amine therefore includes which motor state becomes available and how outputs are coordinated. Structural relatedness does not imply interchangeable physiological action. The experiment establishes responses to applied drugs rather than the timing of natural octopamine or tyramine release during flight choice.

slides.title: Octopamine tunes leg-wing coupling during wind flight
body: Rillich and colleagues retained head input to release fictive flight with wind, then tested how amines changed motor coordination. **Epinastine** is an octopamine receptor antagonist. Leg and wing recordings separated effects on activation from effects on timing during ongoing episodes.

Bath-applied octopamine at 5 mM increased the effectiveness of wind and shortened the cycle. It also tightened the timing of leg motor units relative to wing depressor output, whereas 1 mM epinastine loosened that relationship. Tyramine and its antagonist had no comparable effect on coupling under the tested conditions.

These observations support octopaminergic modulation of recruitment and coordination. They do not contradict the persistence of initiation after amine depletion: facilitation and obligatory activation are different causal roles. The experiment did not directly localize the receptor responsible for coupling to a single CPG neuron.

slides.title: DUM neurons regulate metabolic readiness of flight muscle
body: **Dorsal unpaired median neurons**, or DUM neurons, are centrally located modulatory neurons with peripheral projections. Mentel and colleagues stimulated DUM axons supplying flight muscle M119 in _Locusta migratoria_. Their experiment separated modulatory input from the motor-neuron input that produces contraction.

After unilateral denervation, 1 Hz DUM stimulation for 20 min increased muscle **fructose 2,6-bisphosphate**, a regulator that promotes glycolysis. Its amount rose approximately sevenfold relative to the contralateral control muscle. Glycolysis is the pathway that supplies energy by breaking down carbohydrate.

Central modulatory neurons can therefore prepare the muscle’s metabolic state without themselves generating wingbeat contractions. The within-animal comparison supports a peripheral effect of DUM activity. It does not establish that these neurons initiate the flight CPG or remain equally active throughout sustained flight.

slides.title: PKA is required but insufficient for the metabolic effect
body: **Cyclic AMP**, or cAMP, is an intracellular second messenger; **protein kinase A**, or PKA, is an enzyme activated by cAMP that modifies proteins through phosphorylation. Mentel and colleagues assayed PKA activity and the glycolytic regulator after DUM stimulation.

DUM activity increased PKA activity in flight muscle. Applying the PKA inhibitor KT5720 prevented the DUM-associated increase in fructose 2,6-bisphosphate. A cAMP donor increased PKA activity without reproducing the increase in the glycolytic regulator after a 20 min treatment.

PKA signaling is therefore necessary under these test conditions but is insufficient by itself for the metabolic response. A parallel pathway, possibly involving calcium signaling, was proposed but not established. The experiment concerns muscle metabolism, and cannot be transferred directly to muscarinic activation of thoracic CPG neurons.

slides.title: Central generation works with sensory control
body: Wilson’s reduced preparations established that wing motion is unnecessary for a basic central flight rhythm. Ausborn and colleagues tested how experimentally restored tegula input reshapes that rhythm when sensory stimulation depends on the preceding motor cycle.

The central output was slower and less normally organized without the peripheral loop. Feedback near threshold could accelerate the rhythm, while stronger closed-loop input diminished that acceleration or slowed it. Wind supplies activation, and wing-base sensors supply information about the movement that activation produces.

A CPG is therefore part of a sensorimotor system rather than a guarantee of normal movement in isolation. Central drive, synaptic network interactions, receptor-dependent state and reciprocal feedback contribute different functions. The cited preparations establish those distinctions without providing a complete reconstruction of every connection required for intact flight.

transcript: Central generation. Thoracic circuits produce flight-like alternation without phasic wing feedback; intact frequency and control still depend on sensory interaction.
Wind coding. Head hairs encode speed and direction jointly. Interneurons distinguish maintained airflow, direction, recentring and acceleration.
Activation versus rhythm. Tonic 404 drive can release flight, whereas phase-dependent resetting implicates neurons such as 301 and 501 in rhythm generation.
Synaptic mechanism. Delayed excitation can arise through disinhibition. Pharmacology and reversal tests support a mechanism without identifying every intermediate cell or channel.
Chemical state. Muscarinic signaling supports flight initiation; amines facilitate recruitment, timing and coordination rather than constituting an obligatory trigger in the tested preparation.
Feedback and muscle readiness. Closed-loop tegula input alters frequency, and DUM activity regulates muscle metabolism. Neither role replaces the central generator.
